speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a motion under Standing Order 43. One of the most serious challenges of the 1980s is that we are not self-sufficient in crude oil which is becoming a fast depleting asset in spite of accelerated exploration and development. Therefore, Canada will and must become more dependent on other sources of energy, namely, natural gas, coal, electricity, nuclear energy, etc. Therefore, I move:
That in view of the fact that the National Energy Board is more of a regulatory body and has not the staff for assessing the inventory of reserves of Canada's energy, a royal commission be set up for the purpose of taking an inventory in Canada of all the potential and proven reserves of all types of energy, and at the same time estimate Canada's energy needs for the foreseeable future, as the costs of such a process would be small in relation to the revenue derived by governments and the savings to the consumer on prohibitively priced energy.

subtopic: PRICE OF OIL-INCREASE SOUGHT BY PREMIER LOUGHEED

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: PRICE OF OIL-INCREASE SOUGHT BY PREMIER LOUGHEED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question arises out of the meeting which was held between the Prime Minister and Premier Lougheed in Saskatoon on Monday, I understand. Could the Prime Minister inform us if it is true that Premier Lougheed was pressing for a $5 a year increase in the price of a barrel of oil in 1981 and 1982, and could the Prime Minister tell us that those prices are absolutely unacceptable to him, to the House and to the country?

subtopic: PRICE OF OIL-INCREASE SOUGHT BY PREMIER LOUGHEED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the former prime minister will understand that it would not be helpful to negotiations to discuss the content of private discussions, but I can assure him- although I do not think he needs assurance-that he should not believe everything he reads in the newspapers.

subtopic: PRICE OF OIL-INCREASE SOUGHT BY PREMIER LOUGHEED
speechtext:
I do not, Mr. Speaker, but I thought one could believe what the Prime Minister said at the opening meeting of the first ministers in Ottawa. There he indicated to the premiers that the initial preference of the federal government was an annual increase of $6 a barrel. I do not know if that also appeared in the newspapers, Mr. Speaker, but it seems to me that $6 is even worse than the $5 that Premier Lougheed is reputed to be asking for.
Could the Prime Minister tell us that these figures are unacceptable and he would be looking for some increase of the type that our government brought in with the agreement of producing provinces-a couple of dollars a year? This was sufficient then for Alberta and it was sufficient for Saskatchewan, and the cost of living has not increased in speed since then. Why is this kind of agreement not reached now, Mr. Speaker?

subtopic: PRICE OF OIL-INCREASE SOUGHT BY PREMIER LOUGHEED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, 1 can confirm, as I said at the first ministers' conference, that we have scaled-down our original proposal from increases of $3 every six months after 1980 as a result of representations made by other provinces, particularly the province of Ontario. That remains the position.

subtopic: PRICE OF OIL-INCREASE SOUGHT BY PREMIER LOUGHEED
speechtext:
The Prime Minister is telling us he scaled it down from $6 a year. Why was it at $6 a year in the first place? We know that Syncrude, for instance, has told us that to produce a barrel of synthetic oil will cost in the range of between $15 and $20 a barrel. Why would it have to go up $6 a year? Why is it not sufficient to have a price which will permit-as the Prime Minister told me on Tuesday-him to follow his policy of permitting Canada to be self-sufficient? If the producing companies in Syncrude can get a barrel of oil out at $15, why would the price have to go up to $20, $25 or $30?

November 16, 1979
Oral Questions

subtopic: PRICE OF OIL-INCREASE SOUGHT BY PREMIER LOUGHEED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, our goal is to seek an agreement if possible, and to act without agreement if necessary, on a price that will move Canada toward self-sufficiency. The former prime minister will remember from his negotiations that the goal that was struck at that time had to do, not with the rate of increase in terms of dollars but with the rate of increase in relation to the world price.
He will know now that as a result of changes intervening since the agreement which he signed, the price has fallen to something like 62 per cent of the Chicago price, when his goal at the time he was negotiating matters was to bring the Canadian price much closer to the Chicago price.

subtopic: PRICE OF OIL-INCREASE SOUGHT BY PREMIER LOUGHEED
speechtext: Our policy was never to go up to world prices, regardless of what they would be. Our policy was to have a replacement price, and that is stated in Mr. Gillespie's paper of 1976. Why has the Prime Minister departed from that policy? On Tuesday, again, he was saying it is sufficient that we have a price which will bring on production. If the Middle East decides that the price is $100 a barrel, why do we need that price in Canada to bring on production in Canada?

subtopic: PRICE OF OIL-INCREASE SOUGHT BY PREMIER LOUGHEED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as I indicated to the Leader of the Opposition the other day in the House, our goal is not the world price, it is not the Chicago price, but it is a price that allows Canada to achieve conservation, to achieve substitution and to achieve the bringing on of new supplies. I can quite understand the difficulties faced by the Leader of the Opposition, because his position seems to be diametrically opposite to what is stated by the energy spokesman for the official opposition.

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN OIL PRICES-HIGH INTEREST RATES- DETRIMENTAL EFFECT ON ECONOMY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 have a question for the Minister of Finance. He has been quoted as saying that the $2 a barrel annual increase formula is giving oil companies more than they need for exploration and development.
I want to ask him, therefore, if the government will not now withdraw its plans to increase oil prices rapidly to record world levels and, instead, produce a budget that will deal with the need to help our industries to be more effective, productive and efficient and to help lower-income Canadians to deal with the double shock to our economy due to the Conservative government's policies of high interest rates and record increases in energy prices.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister of Finance):
subsubtopic: INCREASES IN OIL PRICES-HIGH INTEREST RATES- DETRIMENTAL EFFECT ON ECONOMY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is too bad the hon. gentleman was not here last night, because he would now understand that there is no high interest

rate policy. There is a high interest rate condition left by the hon. gentleman's government.

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN OIL PRICES-HIGH INTEREST RATES- DETRIMENTAL EFFECT ON ECONOMY
speechtext: If you had been here you would have heard a lot of nonsense.

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN OIL PRICES-HIGH INTEREST RATES- DETRIMENTAL EFFECT ON ECONOMY
speechtext:
My statement was that it is the calculation of our experts that if a price increase was put into effect, not just a $2 a year increase but in excess of that-another $2 or $2.50 a year-those additional revenues would not be needed by the oil and gas industry for energy investment in Canada; they would have sufficient cash flow to make all necessary energy investments. Therefore, we suggested an energy self-sufficiency levy or tax so that the Government of Canada would have some revenue to do the things necessary for the people of Canada, particularly in the energy field.
We also proposed that all the proceeds of that tax be spent on energy-related matters. If by chance it turned out that there was not a sufficient cash flow for the industry, then adjustments would be made, particularly with reference to independent, Canadian-owned firms in the oil and gas industry which we intend to support and favour.

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN OIL PRICES-HIGH INTEREST RATES- DETRIMENTAL EFFECT ON ECONOMY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there is cold comfort in the minister's words for Canadian consumers and small businesses. Speaking of experts, the minister was telling us the other day that other experts now say that our trade figures are $500 million better than he thought. That being the case, does he not realize that this undermines his argument and that of his government that new information about the balance of payments deficit prevented his government from implementing its election pledge to bring interest rates down? Surely the minister must recognize that that pledge must be implemented since that argument has been undermined?

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN OIL PRICES-HIGH INTEREST RATES- DETRIMENTAL EFFECT ON ECONOMY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, that was really not a question. Despite the fact that an oil company did not report as it apparently should have to Statistics Canada, Customs or whomsoever, that it sold about $500 million this year outside of Canada, which boosts their export earnings by that much- which is welcome news in the sense that it improves our current account deficit for this year-our estimate of what the deficit will be, as a result of the economic conditions left to us by the hon. gentlemen opposite, is that it will still be at least $7 billion. Therefore, this $500 million error has no connection in the world with interest rates-none whatsoever. Why the hon. gentleman keeps harping on this matter is beyond me.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO IMPROVE THE LOT OF OLD AGE PENSIONERS AND PERSONS ON FIXED INCOMES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister. In view of the fact that figures recorded in Hansard on November 7, in response to order paper questions of mine, show that more than 54 per
November 16, 1979

cent of all Canadians 65 years of age and over have so little other income that they qualify for the guaranteed income supplement-which means that they are at the poverty line- and in view of the fact that the cost of living increase, which now stands at 9.3 per cent over a year ago, hits very hard at old age pensioners and at others on fixed incomes, will the Prime Minister tell the House what we can do to get the government to take immediate action to assist these people in their struggle with the rising cost of living?

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO IMPROVE THE LOT OF OLD AGE PENSIONERS AND PERSONS ON FIXED INCOMES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are a number of things that members of this House can do to be helpful. I want this House to know that the whole question of the field of pensions is under review. We would welcome suggestions from all members of the House on changes in pension arrangements that would allow us to be more helpful to Canadians in need.
Second, the House could help the government and help the people of the country by understanding that if we are to get the economy in a position where we are able to bring down costs and inflation, we will have to endure, for at least a period of time, a condition relating to high interest rates and relating to costs that none of us welcomes.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO IMPROVE THE LOT OF OLD AGE PENSIONERS AND PERSONS ON FIXED INCOMES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that many of the people on whose behalf I am speaking will not endure long enough to gain from any improvements the government may make down the line-which means that what we are concerned about is immediate action-will the Prime Minister reconsider the negative answers he has given to our requests for a milk subsidy, a bread subsidy, a fair prices commission with power to roll back unjustified cost increases, a cost of living tax credit or doing something about high interest rates?
Will he take action, now, on one or more of these issues so that the people he is asking to endure will have a chance to live while they are still on this earth?

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO IMPROVE THE LOT OF OLD AGE PENSIONERS AND PERSONS ON FIXED INCOMES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with regard to the specific proposals put forward by the hon. member and his party for some time, I have indicated before that we are not prepared to move on those specific proposals. That remains the case. In some cases we think they would be simply bureaucratic and not effective, while in other cases they are measures which we simply think the country cannot afford at this time.
In relation to inflation, which is the critical and basic problem, it is our view that the only way we can get a handle on inflation and begin to move it down generally, consequently bringing the most relief to the people who are most victimized by it, is to endure, now, some of the high interest rates and other economic problems that have to be faced in the shortterm if we are to have long-term solutions.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO IMPROVE THE LOT OF OLD AGE PENSIONERS AND PERSONS ON FIXED INCOMES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am doing my best to keep my cool as the Prime Minister keeps asking the people I am talking about to endure these conditions. Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that the Prime Minister has said "No" to all of our
Oral Questions
suggestions and has made some others that are futuristic, may I ask what one thing this government has done in the 5 Vi months it has been in office to help pensioners and those on fixed incomes to cope with the rising cost of living? Just one.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO IMPROVE THE LOT OF OLD AGE PENSIONERS AND PERSONS ON FIXED INCOMES
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, I can refer, of course, to the action we have taken with the help of the hon. member in relation to the spouse's allowance, which was the first bill this government introduced. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. Early in 1977 the former government ordered a study on federalism which apparently has gone on for about 16 months. In light of the publication of an interim report which amounted to a harsh criticism of Ottawa's attitude toward Quebec, I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether he could assure the House that he will table the ten known studies as soon as possible?

speechtext:

I think the minister answered the request of a reporter for the publication of a summary of that study and did not indicate the officials or departments involved. I am informed that the study touched upon the question of the nature of relations between federal civil servants and those of the province of Quebec. I am informed also that there was a commitment by the former government not to publish this study which contained evidence given by specific officials. We believe we must honour the commitment given by the former government.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, unless I am mistaken, a commitment has been made to the effect that the details of the evidence given by federal civil servants for that study would not be released. This is a commitment we must honour.
Mr. Speaker, the more the Prime Minister speaks about energy policy, the more confused the Canadian public becomes.
You are more confused.
Oh, oh!
Why don't you go dancing?

He said this morning that the policy was to go toward self-sufficiency. I would like to ask the Prime Minister whether the government's policy is still to achieve self-sufficiency by 1990. Secondly, he said that his target was not the Chicago price or the international price.

The hon. member will understand that among the factors to be taken into account in relation to that figure would be the implication of the Syncrude levy.

Mr. Speaker, I regret that the Prime Minister is still not clarifying whether it is going to be 90 per cent or 95 per cent of the Chicago price or the international price. In his answer he said that it would be either the Chicago price or the international price.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: He didn't.

There is a difference between the two. As a supplementary, the Prime Minister, in the statement he tabled in the House and the statement he made at the federal-provincial conference, talked about the self-sufficiency tax. He said at the conference that the government intended to collect 50 per cent of the revenues in excess of $2 a barrel a year. In the House that evening he said that he was thinking of 50 per cent of the profits. Ever since then he has talked one day of the tax on profits and on another day of a tax on revenue.
Can he tell the House whether he has made up his mind as to what he has in mind? Is it a tax on profits, or a tax on gross revenues? At least he should know which is which.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I have a few questions I would like to address this afternoon to the minister responsible for employment and immigration, particularly on the employment side of his department. Later this afternoon some of my colleagues will pursue a line of questioning on matters pertaining to immigration.
I would first of all like to welcome the minister back to the House. We would very much like to have had the opportunity of having him with us on Tuesday when the unemployment statistics came out. However, I understand very well that the minister was in a period of consultation with his provincial counterparts discussing an employment strategy which we hope to see very soon. We, of course, would like to have had him in the House on Tuesday because Tuesday was the first time in 14 months, as I understand it, that the rate of unemployment went up in this country. That is, of course, a source of concern to us, and I am sure it is a source of concern to the minister.
While we are pleased to see the minister consulting with his provincial colleagues, and while we wish him success in these consultations, we would also hope that these consultations be brought to a close as quickly as possible. As the hon. minister knows, we are already up to November 16, the winter period is upon us, and all indications are there that there is going to be

a rather rapid rise in the rate of unemployment over the next few months.
While telling him that we are in agreement with his consultations, and while wishing him success and also requesting that he make haste, we would like to register some concern. While the minister has been in office for five months with the rest of his colleagues, we have seen very little action on the part of the minister or of his colleagues in bringing forward any concrete programs or proposals. We, of course, like the minister, have read the Speech from the Throne, but we still have yet to see any concrete measures taken as a result of that Speech from the Throne, and we are, indeed, anxious to see some of them taken.
Since the minister has taken office the government of his leader has benefited from a low rate of unemployment, a decreasing rate, as I indicated before, over the past 14 months. But since the minister has taken office there have been a number of developments which should encourage the minister to encourage his department to get into the job-creation field as quickly as possible. We have had the recession in the United States and the first effects of that recession on our economy. It is quite clear that the American economy is not going to be picking up very much over the next few months and, of course, that is going to have some very serious effects on our own economy.
We have had these successive increases in the rates of interest, and once again I can only presume that the minister would agree that these increases in the rate of interest are going to have some dampening effect on the Canadian economy, on many sectors of the Canadian economy. Some of these effects have started to manifest themselves through a number of lay-offs which the minister is aware of and which have been brought to his attention and the attention of the government during the course of the question period over the past few weeks.
Our real concern is that in spite of these trends, in spite of these indications of a worsening economic situation, and in spite of the fact that we have had a lot of rhetoric in the Speech from the Throne, the only concrete action we have seen from the minister to date has actually been a reduction in his department's job-creation programs. I understand the minister has wished to transfer some of those funds to other programs within his department, programs with which we are in full agreement. However, we are not in full agreement with the method of financing these programs. We would have preferred to see programs within the immigration side of his department financed by the general revenues of the country, perhaps by moneys that would have come to the minister from the President of the Treasury Board, but we really cannot approve the minister's decision to reduce the job-creation side of his department and to transfer these funds to the immigration side.
Once again, there is no argument whatsoever with the purposes that have been pursued by the minister on the immigration side. We are in full agreement, and in that connection I think the minister has interpreted quite well the
November 16, 1979

desire of the Canadian people to come to the help of people who are coming to this country in rather dire circumstances.
1 would like to hone in on some of these decreases on the job-creation side which have taken place in spite of the international situation of rising oil prices and recession in the United States and increasing lay-offs and interest rates in this country due to the policies which this government has pursued relentlessly in the hope of strengthening the dollar. That, of course, is a valid objective, but once again we do not agree with the decreases that have come about on the job-creation side.
Since the minister took office, the only announcement he has made is that the funding level for the Canada Works program would be decreased to $100 million this year. In doing so the minister has completely eliminated certain provinces from the application of the job-creation program which was initiated by his predecessor. For instance, the province of Ontario received $22 million to fight unemployment within that province last year, but in spite of the fact that the economy of Ontario in general is more buoyant than that of other provinces-with the possible exception of Alberta-there are a number of pockets of unemployment in the province which once benefited from these programs, but they have now been completely eliminated. The minister has actually taken $22 million away from the province of Ontario since he took office.
Moving further west, and if I recall the figures correctly, the province of Manitoba had an unemployment budget of approximately $9 million last year, but this has disappeared from the communities and the areas of high unemployment in that province. In spite of this fact, the minister has decided to take $22 million away from those communities in Ontario, $9 million away from communities in Manitoba and something like $8 million away from communities and unemployed people in the province of Saskatchewan. The story goes on. Last year the contribution to British Columbia was $16 million. This year it is down to almost a pittance in that province. 1 also understand that the amounts have been decreased for the Yukon.

The hon. member has conveniently forgotten a very important program. Since he has so diligently read documents of the previous government, I wonder if the hon. member has heard of LEAP which stands for the Local Employment Assistance Program. 1 wonder if the hon. member would call up some of the Metis and non-status Indian leaders in Manitoba while he is there and ask them whether they have heard of LEAP. I can assure the hon. member that they have heard of LEAP and that there are millions of dollars under this government's program in LEAP funds, not Canada Works funds, going into Manitoba to help those who want jobs.
These people do not want the short-term, make-work, government job-creation projects of the previous administration. They want permanent, meaningful jobs that will produce real

goods and services in the economy, real life jobs that the previous government was unable to produce. I would suggest that the LEAP allocation, which is a mere $18 million for this fiscal year and a mere $12 million for the next fiscal year-all of which the hon. member conveniently forgot to mention- will provide long-term jobs in three-year projects to a great many disadvantaged people throughout the country. These are the very people who need work, who have not been able to get it under the previous government and who will get it under this government.
How many jobs?

I will give the hon. member his due. The previous government created the program but they did not push it hard enough. They were so preoccupied with the politics of constituency allocations in Canada that they ignored the forest for the trees. I suggest that while the Canada Works program has led to some useful projects, it is one of the most expensive projects for job creation in the history of this country. The taxpayer has not had value for his dollar. If we look at the cost of each Canada Works job under phase 3 of the previous administration, we will find that the costs came close to $11,000 per job.
Where do those jobs go? With minimum allocation in every constituency, do they go to the hon. member's friends? Were they allocated on a political basis or did they get real jobs for people who were in real need?
I have suggested that some of those projects were good. Some in this phase, coming from the constituencies of hon. members opposite, will be good. Nevertheless, that program had inherent deficiencies and I believe the hon. member knows that. While it may have had some utility in the early and mid-seventies as the successor to LIP, its days are over. We must look now toward long-term job creation where people can guarantee that they have a job, and that the jobs in many cases will not come from direct government job creation but from the private sector, which the previous government never realized was the real producer of goods and services in a society.
Why did you cut the LEDA program? That was the private sector. You cut that.

I know the minister will say that part of what I say will be a repetition of some of the discussions that he and I have had, partly through correspondence and partly in committee. This is the first opportunity, however, to get the discussion on the record in Parliament so that people can see what is actually happening.
Since the minister agreed a moment or two ago that it is likely we will have more unemployment in this country in the coming months than we have had, as shown by the increase in the numbers and rates we got just a few days ago, that increase in unemployment will come inevitably because the United States is already in a recession. The effects of that recession must increase the number of unemployed in this country. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I say to the minister that the decision made by this government to reduce funding for employment programs from $175 million to $100 million this year was a mistake of major proportions.
I want to examine what has happened, Mr. Chairman. The government made a decision that the Canada Works program in Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia should be eliminated completely, the reason being that the rate of unemployment in those provinces was relatively low. That is true for the provinces as a whole, Mr. Chairman, but in each of those provinces members, regardless of party, and the minister should know that there are important pockets of unemployment, particularly among young people and native people. The minister knows, or should know, that the very large number of unemployed native people, those who live on reserves, are not even counted in the figures which Statistics Canada prepare on unemployment. In all these provinces, therefore, the rate of unemployment is much higher than the figure shown. That was ignored when the minister made his decision.
Since the member for Blainville-Deux-Montagnes referred to Manitoba, let me spend a few moments dealing with what actually happened there. The minister made a great deal of how the increase in LEAP funds has satisfied and pleased the leaders of the native communities, the status and non-status Indians. I want to tell the minister that his information is wrong and to put the figures that we have on the record. I know the minister will say that I am using a different set of figures; I am using the fiscal year while he used the calendar year. The minister cannot deny, however, that there has been a substantial reduction in the amount of money available in the province of Manitoba for employment programs. We got our figures from his department. They show that for the year 1978-79, $9.5 million, in round figures, was allocated to the province of Manitoba for Canada Works programs. There was $2,300,000 for LEAP programs. That is a total of $11,779,000. Of that $11 million plus, under Canada Works for native

November 16, 1979
Supply
programs there was $6.5 million, and through LEAP for native employment programs there was $1,300,000. So we had $11.75 million in total for employment programs in Manitoba and $7,800,000 in round figures for native programs. This year we will have no Canada Works money, and we will have only $5.5 million for LEAP programs. According to my calculations, that is a reduction of over $6 million and a reduction in native programs of $4.5 million.
The minister has an explanation. It is not quite as bad as I have indicated, and I hope he will put it on the record, but the fact is that the $5.5 million which is available is substantially less than was available last year. How does this work? The minister talks about constituency allocations as though they were pork barrel allocations. I do not know how it has worked in other provinces, but I know how it works in our province.
The constituency of Churchill, which was represented by a Conservative member of Parliament last year so I am sure there was no pork barrelling then, has a very large number of native people. Churchill's total allocation last year was $3,900,000, of which $3,300,000 went for native programs. With a total of $5.5 million available for the whole province for all employment programs, native and non-native, with areas in which the native people have unemployment rates at certain times of the year running as high as 90 per cent, how can the minister say they are satisfied?
Let us take the city of Winnipeg as an example. Winnipeg has a large number of native people living there. Probably more native people live in Winnipeg than in any other area in the country. Last week we had a report that stated that in the core area of Winnipeg there are 6,000 native children attending school; we are talking about a population of 20,000 people.
Last year the constituency represented by my colleague the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and my own constituency received total allocations of about $2.25 million, of which about $1.25 million was for native programs. I can tell the minister that 1 spoke to his office about 20 minutes ago. The information given to me last week was confirmed by his office, that the total number of native programs approved and funded in Winnipeg was four. I know that the rate of unemployment in Winnipeg is low, but I want to tell the minister that the rate of unemployment among native people in Winnipeg is very high. These people have the poorest level of education. Now is not the time to give all the figures, but I can tell him that these people have the poorest housing and the poorest health standards. So when the government cuts back the way it did, it is attacking the people who are already the poorest in this country.
Shame.

I say to the minister that what the government did is inexcusable. What we needed was not less money but more money.
Since I have a plane to catch this afternoon, I will take a few more minutes to raise two other questions which 1 hope
[Mr. Orlikow.)
the minister can deal with when I am not here, but 1 will certainly come back to him in committee.
We are spending hundreds of millions of dollars through the department on manpower training. I have a figure here of expenditures for last year of $738 million, which we arrived at by totalling the amount of money spent for the purchase of training seats in the community colleges, income support for trainees, industrial training, on the job programs and the allowance to those on unemployment insurance benefits. The minister may argue about that figure, but it is certainly in the hundreds of millions of dollars.
1 want to read one paragraph to the minister from a study commissioned by the minister of labour in the last government. It was given to this minister of labour a few weeks ago. This was a study headed by Dr. Adams; I believe he is from McMaster University. At page 117 of this report, which is entitled "Education and Working Canadians-Report of the Commission of Inquiry on Educational Leave and Productivity", the board reports as follows:
Despite free and generally available access, there are an estimated one million Canadians who cannot read or write. Another four million are said to be functionally illiterate-that is, they cannot read, write and do mathematics at a level necessary to function adequately in society.
I know education under our constitution is the responsibility of the provinces. But manpower training, which is so essential if people are going to get jobs-people who are unemployed and not qualified to get adequate jobs-is the responsibility of the federal government and the minister's department. I quoted from this report, but the board did not come up with figures we did not know about before. Despite this record- one cannot blame him because he was not the minister then, but I bring it to his attention and hope that if he cannot give me an answer today, he will give some thought to it-his department each year has been cutting back on the funds made available for basic education upgrading. Those programs are most needed by our native people, who have been undereducated, and by our immigrants, so many of whom in recent years have come from countries where their language is not English. They are also needed by wives of immigrants who cannot function very well in our society because of lack of ability to speak either of our official languages.
So I want to put it to the minister today that his department needs to rethink its whole approach to the training of people who are unskilled and who desperately need training. These are the people who are being short-changed more each year than they were in previous years with the inadequate funding that we had then.
I believe I have about five more minutes. I would like to call it one o'clock, Mr. Chairman, and take my five minutes when we come back from the lunch period.

Mr. Chairman, I want to go back for a minute or two to the question of Canada Works. If the minister checks with the officials in his department, he will be told that the advisory committee appointed by my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, and myself to go over the applications in past years for our two constituencies consisted of people active in various community groups. They will also tell him that on not one occasion did we ask the officials in his department or the members of the advisory committee to favour one application over another. We took the view that they were competent and would judge on the basis of the best applications.
I want to put on record part of a newsletter which came to me from the King Edward community school. That school is located in the working class part of my constituency. There are a large number of native people and a large number of new Canadians in the area. One page in the newsletter is entitled "No more Canada Works jobs". 1 will read a couple of paragraphs:
-Canada Works no longer exists!!! One of the first things the new federal government did after the May election was cut all Canada Works grants in Manitoba. There will be no new Canada Works projects in Manitoba this year.
At King Edward over the last two years we have employed 11 people (most of them from our own neighbourhood) on Canada Works grants-
They then list some of the projects included in their program, such as classroom teacher aides, lunch and after school program, senior citizen worker, adult education programs, aides to work on the monthly newsletter, community resource booklet, aides to assist the community group and its committees, etc. So that is what the minister and his government have accomplished with their cut-off of Canada Works programs, and that example could be duplicated in nearly every constituency in the country.

I want to raise one more matter with the minister, and that is that despite the fact that we have had very large efforts and spent hundreds of millions of dollars on manpower training, it is now obvious that we do not have in this country the skilled workers who are needed. For example, when General Motors announced that it was going to build a new plant, it had to get permission from the government and it got permission from the government to go overseas to Europe to recruit skilled workers. I find it very strange after all these years and these very large expenditures that we do not have the skilled workers who are needed.
I have here a document entitled "Manpower Requirements and Hiring Plans of Ontario Employers in Manufacturing Industries" prepared by the Ontario Manpower commission. Because 1 have very little time I want to read just one paragraph. This document says, and I quote:

Out of the many hundreds of specific comments made by employers on the causes of their recruitment difficulty-
And there were 250 occupations they could not find people for.
-there emerges a virtual consensus-a general lack of proper training in the industrial trades ... Many employers think that the education system has failed to produce the industrial skills and problem-solving ability that they need; too much emphasis is being given to university training, and only the less-intelligent and ambitious students are being encouraged to enter trade courses.
I know that education until the end of high school is a provincial responsibility, but manpower training is the responsibility of the federal government, and I say there is something fundamentally wrong with our system and with our department if after all these years and the expenditure of literally billions of dollars we are still not able to produce the kind of skilled manpower which is required.
1 know that apprenticeship courses come under the jurisdiction of the provinces, but I suggest to the minister that it is time he and his department got together with provincial ministers and decided co-operatively and jointly to establish apprenticeship programs in co-operation with employers and unions so that we do not, after all these years, have to import skilled workers as we are doing at the present time. It seems to me that that period should have long since expired. We have the ability now, if we use our means properly, to reduce the number of skilled workers who are needed now and who will be needed even more if we get the economy working at full capacity, as it should be.

Mr. Chairman, I just want to put on record some what I think are cogent facts concerning the province of Manitoba. Manitoba is an important province which 1 had the great honour to visit as recently as yesterday morning and to meet with the minister of labour and manpower of that province in order to co-ordinate better our respective employment programs in anticipation of the events of 1980.
I was delighted to hear the hon. member speak on the subject of training. The estimates of this government for the current fiscal year show that in institutional training we have increased the budget from the previous year from a sum last year of $23.3 million under the previous government to the sum of $24.4 million. Industrial training receives a rather more substantial increase proportionately, from $2.9 million to the sum of $5 million. That is a recognition of the importance of training throughout Canada and in particular in the province of Manitoba.
Finally, I want to say in relation to the hon. member's comments concerning-

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman. I think that the name of my distinguished colleague appeared before mine on the list and that he was supposed to be recognized before I was. He was here in the House this morning.

Mr. Chairman, 20 minutes is not very much time for all the questions to which 1 had been hoping to get answers from this minister, and with his co-operation 1 would like to use the 20 minutes to ask pointed questions and hopefully to receive answers from him.
The first area 1 want to explore is an interpretation which I have taken from the annual report to Parliament on immigration levels for 1980 in which 1 detect from hon. members opposite, particularly the Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport and Multiculturalism, an air of aggrieved misrepresentation; so I want to ask the minister a few questions about it to make sure that 1 do properly understand it as representing a change in direction, with respect to family class and assisted relatives, from that taken in the past.
Let me direct the minister's attention to page 33 of his report, which he tells us he wrote himself. Although there are many words of comfort in it designed to comfort, if not to mislead, members of the various communities of Canada who may be interested in having their family members join them in Canada, I want simply and pointedly to ask the minister a question. When the minister says in that statement that he will be increasing the proportion of immigrants who are selected against economic criteria-that is, the independent immigrants-knowing that the refugee class is not to be decreased, if the proportion of immigrants selected against economic criteria is to be increased, which classes of immigrants are to be decreased proportionately?

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member makes a rather spurious assumption that, because you have a reorientation of balance, necessarily one group must be decreased in numbers. The report is very clear that the principle of family reunification will continue to govern the admission of close family members, and 1 want to assure the hon. member and other

hon. members of my commitment to the principle of family reunification and to maintaining the family class in terms of the number of admissions.
That is to suggest that the other classes-assisted relatives, which the hon. member well knows involves economic criteria, and the independent class of immigrants-may well, in order to right the balance, if you will, have to be increased as a result in 1981, 1982 and the years in the future in order to meet the labour market demand which is ever present in our society and, I suggest, will be even more present in 1981, 1982 and 1983 as we develop mega projects, particularly in the Canadian west. 1 suggest in response to the hon. member that we have a need for a greater number of immigrants selected against economic criteria in order to meet legitimate labour market demands in this country.

As I understand the format, the minister and I can continue for 20 minutes.
We now have from the minister an indication that you can have a base quantity in which all components can increase in proportion. 1 want to suggest to the minister that that is just absurd, that if one proportion of a group of components is increased, it necessarily follows that the other proportions have to decrease. So I want to ask him again which proportion is decreasing to provide room for the increase in the proportion of people who are selected on the basis of the economic criteria.

Mr. Chairman, I will be very brief because 1 believe that the member's question was answered previously. 1 am prepared to continue the current level of family reunification, family class cases, in terms of their numbers. At the same time, we can have a reorientation of the balance to reflect current economic needs in this country. What could be clearer than that?
1 would just ask the minister the following question. It does not make sense to me that you can maintain the component of refugees-which is not at issue-or even increase it-
Don't ask about refugees.

I am putting that aside. But that the minister can maintain the proportion of the family class and yet increase the proportion of immigrants brought in under economic criteria does not make any sense to me. If one component in the total is being increased proportionately, something has to be decreased proportionately, and I put to him that if it is not the family class, it is the assisted relatives class that he is proposing to decrease. 1 want to ask him if that is not the only possible way of interpreting the orientation about which he is talking.

Given the suggested reorientation-and 1 want to make it clear we are talking about future years-and given the operation of immigrant processes, the likelihood of using
November 16, 1979

labour market criteria to increase the balance on the other side of the ledger will and could result in an increase in the number of both assisted relatives and independent immigrants, depending on the circumstances and depending on where the applications for admission to Canada come from, what persons apply, with what skills and education, and other qualifications. The hon. member is fully aware of the immigration processes and the use of economic criteria to equate demand for entry into Canada with economic need from within Canada. It is a fairly simple proposition and 1 fail to see his confusion.

I am not confused. I understand very well what the problem is. The problem is that if you have a given total which will be determined every year on November 1 for the year ahead, and you want to increase the proportion of those who are chosen by economic criteria, you will inevitably be decreasing the proportion of those who are not, and those are in the family class and assisted relatives class. I do not see how the country can draw any other interpretation from it.
1 should like to ask one final question on that subject before moving on to some of the manpower problems in the manpower department, not national manpower problems but staff problems. However, before I move on to that subject, I have one final observation to make about this issue, and that is to ask whether this new government is following the practice of having the minister of multiculturalism participate in the making of the decision to increase the proportion of economically chosen immigrants. I ask that question as well because the minister of multiculturalism, in his answer to a question that I asked, indicated that he had read the document on the 1980 immigration levels. I was delighted to hear that he had read it but I was disappointed to draw from that the conclusion that he had not had an important hand in the drafting and setting of those ceilings in an area which should be of great concern to him and to his portfolio.

Mr. Chairman, the minister of state for multiculturalism and I consult on a regular basis. As part of the government we are fully in accord with decisions that each of us takes. I have no hesitation in giving the hon. member the assurance that the level of family class immigration under the Liberal government in 1978, which amounts to 46,218, will be maintained by the present government. 1 would also have no hesitation in giving him the assurance that the level of assisted relatives, numbering 18,019 in 1978, is generally a level which will be maintained. He has those assurances and I can do no better than to give him the specific numbers from the most recent record of the government which he supported prior to May 22. The assurances are there and there is no reason for going about the country suggesting there will somehow be a decrease or lessening of commitment to the principle of family reunification. The record is clear.

I think that now we are coming closer to the point. I have the statistics to which the minister referred. I did not suggest that the number of family class people or the number of assisted relatives might be reduced, and I am glad to hear it will not be. What I asked was whether the proportion
Supply
would be reduced. In 1978 they numbered 86,000-odd admissions to Canada. The target for 1979 was higher and the result was higher. The target for 1980 is higher. If the minister intends to keep the family and assisted relatives class, if I can put it that way, at the low level at which they were in 1978 in relation to others, then he will indeed be reducing the proportion of that class. If he regards 46,232 or the other number that he used, which was slightly different, for family and assisted relatives class as the total which will be permitted in the 1980 quota or level, then he is indeed reducing the proportion although he maintains the absolute numbers-the proportion will be going down.
This would be consistent with other evidence which he gave before the committee which I have here. I can refer to proceedings of the meetings of the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration at page 140 in the report in which he expressed concern that the family class had been growing as a proportion, and I took from his report some indication that he was going to do something about it. I conclude from the answer he has just given that indeed he has and he wants to see, whatever the absolute numbers are, a reduction in the proportion of the family and assisted relatives class. This is quite different from the policies of the former government, and I think he ought to say so.

Mr. Chairman, I am surprised to see the hon. member draw a comparison between 1978 and 1979-80, suggest that the figures are higher for 1979-80 and that somehow the numbers of family class people to which I made a commitment will therefore be proportionately smaller. He knows the reason that the numbers for 1979-80 are higher. The reason is the special refugee program from southeast Asia. Is the hon. member coming to this House at this late stage saying that he is suddenly opposed to the program of bringing refugees from southeast Asia? I thought I heard the hon. member suggesting last summer that we should have done better than accepting only 50,000 refugees over two years, and that personally he would have preferred to see the number go up to 100,000. I heard the hon. member say that in public on a number of occasions. Quite naturally, if you bring in a large number of refugees, which happens to be the single largest refugee movement in Canadian history, the proportion of other classes will go down. That is nothing new and I am not ashamed to say that. What really counts is the number of human beings who can come to this country and join their families, their husband, their wife, their children. We will maintain the numbers.

I look forward to seeing that happen, but I will believe it when I see it. I have no change to make in my own ideas about refugees. I am delighted with the results of our policy on refugees and, as the minister noted, I have said so on many occasions.
I want to turn now in the very few minutes I have left to some of the staffing problems that have come to our attention in his department. I know that he has undertaken, under a directive of the President of the Treasury Board, to try to find $117 million in his immigration portfolio to pay for the

November 16, 1979
Supply
refugee program. Part of this has come from outside that envelope and he explained that before the committee. But I am very concerned that part of it also is coming from a reduction in the level of staffing within the immigration department. Ele gave figures to us which have taken some time to understand but, as 1 understand them, there is a reduction in the staff at the Toronto international airport and there are some reductions elsewhere.
I want to ask him, again pointedly, if he can give us some idea as to where he will find the rest of that $117 million. For example, in some of our immigration offices in India, in a family reunification case of a husband or wife here bringing a spouse over to Canada as a landed immigrant, one must wait three or four months to receive an answer to a letter and well over a year before any reunification results. I have had a lot of such experiences in my own constituency; perhaps the minister has as well. I would assert that this shocking delay is caused by lack of adequate staffing in our missions.
The minister received the mandate from his colleague to cut and cut until he comes up with $117 million. How will he do it? Does the minister not agree, instead of asking for reductions in staffing with his responsibilities in immigration in his department, that in fact he should be asking for increased staff, not only so that processing can be done more expeditiously, but so that there can be better policing?
One thing which discredits immigration is the presence of many illegal immigrants in the country. Part of the answer to that is more adequate staffing in immigration, so that more attention can be paid to immigration flow. However well meaning they are, I do not think his staff are in a position to do their jobs as efficiently as they could because of simple overwork in many, many locations in Canada and around the world.
What resolution has been made of the problem recently brought to my attention by the union local of Vancouver international airport immigration officials concerning a problem which was public knowledge toward the end of the last Parliament? Members of the union at the Vancouver international airport were complaining that they were underpaid relative to immigration officials working in other immigration centres across the country. Also they were understaffed relative to their workload in comparison to others. I remember the former minister saying that this problem would be looked into, and that some attention would be paid to it in part by the Treasury Board. What has the minister done in an attempt to resolve some of this feeling of ill-will developing within the ministry because of these pressures?

Mr. Chairman, I will attempt to be brief in giving the hon. member some of the information he requires. First I should like to say in support of the immigration staff, particularly at the major ports of entry into Canada, and at some of the busier missions abroad such as New Delhi, that they are first class staff. They work hard, they work long hours, and they serve well Canada and the new people coming

to this country. They are devoted public servants. I will defend each and every one of them.
At Toronto international airport there are 45 immigration employees in terminal one and 51 employees in terminal two. There is one staff vacancy in terminal one and two staff vacancies in terminal two. There are seven officers assigned to the New York office. In addition, there are three immigration program officers who are engaged locally in support of the work of our foreign service officers. I admit that there are some problems in New Delhi into which I will be looking in greater depth. There were seven Canadian-based officers and two locally-based officers in 1977. This complement is being maintained through 1978-1979, despite cuts in other areas where business has slackened off somewhat.
1 should like to address myself to the problem, apparently, in Vancouver to which the hon. member made reference. I may say in all candour that, in my lengthy discussions with the former minister during the transitional period, he did not think it was sufficiently important to raise it with me. Officials have not brought that problem to my attention since, nor have the Vancouver staff made direct representations to me as a result. Nevertheless, if there is a problem of staff being underpaid or having a too onerous workload, 1 will undertake to the hon. member and that staff to look into the situation and do my very level best to improve working conditions for them. Probably they are the second, if not the third, busiest port of entry into Canada, and they deserve every support I can give.

speechtext: 1 regret to advise the hon. member for York Centre that his time has expired.

Mr. Chairman, 1 should like to put some questions especially about job-creation programs for young people. We know that the throne speech stated that the government intended to organize special programs for them and to set up offices. Now this is my first question: I should like to ask the minister if this new job-creation program for young people will take off something from existing programs which were part of the employment strategy already in effect or if the funds will merely be cut off from the present program and earmarked for those new programs? And then, Mr. Chairman, 1 would also like to know if estimates for the integration program of young university graduates will be available under that program, since the private business sector advises me that there are no such funds in the Montreal area? That is my first question.

Mr. Chairman, currently there is a program for young people which is a structured program established under the previous government. Some aspects of that program are still continuing and will continue through until the end of this fiscal year, that is up until the end of March, 1980. Some aspects of that program have been more successful than others. In particular, I would mention the employment tax credit program which, while slow to start, has become very popular
November 16, 1979

and very successful, perhaps in the province of Quebec more than in any other province. It is a happy example of private sector employers working together with Canada employment officers and young people seeking work to get more young people into the work force in permanent jobs which are private sector based. That is a good thing, and we may well draw some lessons from the experience of that particular program.
However, I may say that the program of the government, the details of which will be indicated in the budget and the budget debate, in fact will be a new one. There are many aspects to it. It is premature for me to indicate the details of that program in advance of the budget announcement. However, I can indicate to the hon. member that there will be greater emphasis on long-term job creation for young people. We will attempt to receive greater value for the dollars spent to get more young people into the work force. There will be a new emphasis on young people which perhaps transcends that of the previous government. Finally, it will be a program which will have the support of the provincial governments across Canada. It will be co-ordinated with their youth programs in a way that perhaps programs of the previous government were not.
In so far as the job integration program is concerned, I will have to take that question under advisement and get back to the hon. member with greater details. I do not have the information required by the hon. member immediately at my disposal.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to discuss with the minister a very important subject, and more particularly the Canada Works program. The minister certainly has an extremely complicated department, and I can understand that immigration, manpower and unemployment are areas in which people are extremely interested. I believe that the results we have been able to see so far indicate that the minister has tried to make a rather equitable distribution across Canada. And yet in July this year, if you remember, the minister announced the fourth phase of the Canada Works program which included substantial cuts in certain ridings and extremely heavy ones in others.
If I look, for example, at the formula the minister used to make those cuts in the Canada Works program, more particularly in the riding of Bonaventure-Oes-de-la-Madeleine, using the minister's figures, I see the rate of surplus manpower in that riding was 32.4 per cent. Using that figure, the riding of Bonaventure-Iles-de-la-Madeleine should have received for this year $5,333,000 under the Canada Works program. If one looks at the way the Canada Works program has evolved over the last four years, one sees that in the first phase we should have got $1,433,000, during the second, $3,855,000, and during the third, $3,132,000. The minister may think that $3 million is a lot for a riding, and I can understand that in certain ridings it can mean a lot, but in the Gaspe area, more particularly in the riding of Bonaventure-lles-de-la-Madeleine,
Supply
that is not enough, particularly when based on the department's figures: $5,333,000 was being recommended and following the policy set by the department, that was cut to $3 million.
I would also like to point out to the minister that all those Canada Works projects that were carried out in past years were extremely important to us. Take, for example, construction, development, recreation, research services. Also, we were able to complete works in the riding that could not be carried out with the normal budgets of federal departments in our area and even more in the case of certain municipalities under certain provincial government programs. That is to say that those amounts of money from the Canada Works program provided the people in our area with services, developments that could not be paid for by any other means.
Another major concern in my constituency is the fact that we have three Canada manpower centres. There is the Causap-scal sector, the New Richmond sector, the Chandler sector and the Magdalen Islands sector, and the sums allocated to these three ridings have been distributed according to the population and the number of unemployed. When the minister makes a decision to allocate funds to the various constituencies, I would like him to note and to consider two major points, namely that the sums allocated to each part of the Bonaventure-Iles-de-la-Madeleine constituency are actually allocated according to the unemployment rate and the population.
I should like to come back to what I said earlier about Canada Works this year. Hon. members will recall that in July the minister sent them a communique informing them of the new formula and the new philosophy of Canada Works projects, and that he underlined, perhaps rightly, that this year he had decided to abolish the advisory committees so that, as we understand it, hon. members would have more opportunity to make recommendations concerning the applications received. Mr. Chairman, 1 will deal with the two questions that the member has raised, in reverse order. Fisrt of all dealing with the approval authority as a general proposition, let me say to him that I take all the advice that I can get from every source. I talk to approval authorities, my project officers in the regions where the projects come from-
In Jerusalem.

That was unnecessary, my friend. I talk to hon. members opposite as well. I have had very good submissions in a very non-partisan way from persons who have gone into these communities and tried to assist the government in determining which projects, at a time of scarce resources, are the best projects to serve the community. I had my own project officers, many of whom have had experience now through four phases of Canada Works programs, as well as having experience in some cases with the local initiatives program. Of course, I have my own officials here in Ottawa as well as hon. members on all sides of the House. It is a process which ultimately ends up on my desk, and I take full responsibility.
As was pointed out by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre earlier, there was in previous phases an intermediate mechanism in the circuit called the minister's advisory board.
November 16, 1979

It used to be called a constituency advisory group. I felt that, given the time available and the excellent rapport and communications channels which I have from so many sources, perhaps it was an unnecessary and overly bureaucratic process which did not necessarily assist the community, let alone assist the minister and the government in the decisions which had to be taken. 1 do want to give a list of the persons who in a formal way are consulted, including members of Parliament, local resource persons, the provincial governments, relevant federal departments and agencies.
The hon. member will recall this morning that reference was made to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and his department where in some areas of the Atlantic provinces and Quebec applications of the type affecting small craft harbours are seriously considered in that particular context. The employment development branch officials within CEIC, other officials within my department and the local employment assistance program officials are often consulted, particularly if there is any aspect of native involvement in a Canada Works project.
I think it is a good process, and I am hopeful that the projects that have been approved and that will be approved, with the scarce dollars available for this year, will be of service to the country in the primary function of getting unemployed people into the work force.
To answer the first question, which is a good one, regarding the $3 million going to the hon. member's constituency where there is a very high labour surplus rate, I appreciate that the labour surplus rate is 32.4 per cent, which is one of the highest in Canada. While this is not a good situation, I am sure the hon. member will realize that, given a total program budget of $100 million and an allocation to his province of almost half that amount, there had to be some reasonable ceiling on a per constituency basis to make sure that all the funds were not drained into one constituency or region.
The previous government was prepared to consider a variety of options-before the events of May 22 intervened-one of them being the option which I selected. There were other options but I can assure the hon. member that the $3 million ceiling was not intended to deprive his region of moneys that are rightfully theirs. 1 am merely trying to share the money in a way that best fits the unemployment needs of these regions in Canada where unemployment is high, and the province of Quebec is no exception in that regard.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to come back to the matter of the minister's decision with regard to the choice of projects under the Canada Works program. The minister mentioned in his reply, and rightly so, I believe, that his officials and the various other government groups were making suggestions to him. But let us come back to the Gaspe Peninsula and the Lower St. Lawrence area where the minister has civil servants there on the spot on duty with the various manpower centres, and to Rimouski where his representatives
Supply
are required to go out and meet with the groups and organizations concerned who may have representations to make.
The hon. member, the manpower centre, the regional employment centre have all made the same recommendation to the minister and, according to my information, the latter seems to have ignored those recommendations. It also seems he changed the amounts or the projects involved. Can the minister tell the House where he got the other information because, as he mentioned and as I pointed out a while ago, I feel his officials are, so to speak, in a better position and more knowledgeable to make an assessment of those projects. If such recommendations differ from those submitted by the hon. member and the manpower centre, perhaps the minister could justify the reasons which motivated him into making that change, and tell us where he got that other information?

Mr. Chairman, as I have indicated, I attempt to get all the information I possibly can about projects that are coming forward in the form of application. As the hon. member knows, there are far more projects than there are moneys available. The decisions which must be taken are very difficult. If I were to sit down and provide reasons and justification for every project that was either rejected or reduced in amount, I would be working 24 hours a day, seven days a week on Canada Works projects alone. If I had the time, certainly that might be a justifiable exercise, but it is a very difficult process to meet all the demands of hon. members and project officers of local communities. I do the best job I can under the circumstances.
There is also a time element to consider. We are very anxious to get as many approvals through this year as possible, rather than have the moneys go over to the next fiscal year. The more money we can get out in the form of people taking jobs, the less agony there will be in the hon. member's constituency and other constituencies. So I take all the input available and make the best judgments I can. The hon. member and I can argue as to the merits and demerits of each individual project. But the nature of the system is such that the ultimate decision is mine, and I accept that responsibility. 1 give my best assurance to the hon. member, and to all members of the House, that I do the best I can with the resources I have available, but it is a very difficult job. I sincerely believe, based on past performance, that we can allocate those moneys fairly and that we can get people into the work force, which is the primary objective.

Mr. Chairman, 1 rise on a point of order. I wonder if I might make a suggestion which will be of some service to hon. members on this side, as well as to members on all sides perhaps, including you, Mr. Chairman. Mr. Chairman, I should like to return briefly and to thank the hon. member for Nickel Belt for this consideration, and then resume the line of questioning I was on before.
I was very pleased to hear the minister's hearty endorsement of his officials. He is taking a very different attitude toward them now that he knows them, than the attitude he took when he first assumed his responsibilities. He did not indicate to me or to the House where he would find the $117 million that his colleague, the President of the Treasury Board, has asked him to cut from his department. 1 wonder, first, if he would be prepared to assure this House that those cuts will not come in the form of reduced staffing and, indeed, that the reduction of staffing that I referred to will be reversed and at least the complement restored to what it was at the beginning of 1979.
I want to inquire about two other matters very briefly, as I do not want to encroach unduly on the time of other members. It has been disclosed in newspaper columns, particularly in The Globe and Mail of October 9, that 20 per cent of landed immigrants in Canada at the time the article was written, received their landed immigrant status through special order. I know that this is the result of a practice of the government. I am not suggesting that the granting of a minister's permit in any particular case was improper. I have often sought them myself, upon representations from my riding. I think in every individual case, let us say, it is proper that a minister's permit be issued.
The system is a bad one, however, when such a heavy reliance on intervention at the political level is required. I want
[Mr. Blaker.j
to ask the minister whether consideration is being given to changing the system to some method where there would be less intervention and more of the system working to produce the kind of results which we see for legal immigration and for landed immigrant statuts, and about which I am not making any complaint at this time.
Finally, I think the country may be interested to know how the Canadian Foundation for Refugees is doing and how much public support it has managed to attract to date in the form of contributions.

Dealing with the last question first, Mr. Chairman, I will be meeting tomorrow with the co-chairman, Mr. Mitchener, of the Canadian Foundation for Refugees. I hope to have more information at that time to provide the hon. member with the information he requires.
I can indicate to him, however, that with my encouragement the directors of that fund have been very cautious so as to not appear to be, or in fact to be, competing with other valid and genuine fund-raising efforts in the voluntary sector. They have been co-ordinating their activities so that they are meshing their existing and planned activities with some very successful operations in the private sector. I think that is a very responsible way of proceeding.
Dealing with the question of minister's permits, the figures to which the hon. member refers relate to the experience of the previous government and my predecessor. While he may be sanguine that this is a good system and is not worried about 20 per cent, I must tell him that I am. As the one who is holding this discretionary power, I worry from time to time that, when dealing with human beings, in leaving that sort of power vested in one person and with the amount of delegation that entails, there may be a serious problem of unfettered discretion in our law which requires examination.
I hope this is one area in which the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration may be of assistance to me and to the government in finding ways to contain the granting of minister's permits. I do not mean to reduce in any way the compassion or discretion in genuine cases of need, but to provide an element of consistency and fairness so that people will know and live by the rules. We must make sure that it is not immigration perceived as "who you know", but perceived more as what the fair rules, open for all people, are.
Finally, to deal with the question of staff cuts and the cost of the refugee program, the hon. member well knows that that $117 million is now estimated to be more in the order of $110 million. At least half of those funds will be required in fiscal year 1980-81. Of course that is not before us today as the estimates for 1980-81 have not been prepared. This is a program carrying on through to the end of 1980, as the hon. member well knows. I will indicate the areas of progress in that respect.
Dealing with the reallocation within this fiscal year, this subject was discussed before the standing committee. There was some $17.7 million in job creation funds in programs of the previous government, which had not been expended, not-
November 16, 1979

withstanding that the programs had terminated. It seems to me that if there are funds which have been allocated to programs which have terminated and, by definition, were therefore not necessary or their full extent was not necessary, then the financially prudent thing to do was not to go out and borrow money by increasing the deficit, but to take those unused funds and reallocate them for what I think the hon. member would agree is a very useful purpose.
Just to repeat, Mr. Chairman, some $7.5 million in the job experience training program was not taken up when the program expired, by the edict of the former government, on May 31, 1979. Do we just let that money lapse or do we use it wisely? I suggest the latter.
Some $4.7 million set aside in the portable wage subsidy program was not taken up. The intent of that program was to assist the re-employment of workers laid off as a result of any trade or tariff changes. As a result of those changes, those funds were not required. Surely the hon. member is not suggesting it was imprudent to reallocate those funds to what he says is a worth-while program.
Finally, some $6 million was allocated for training allowances but was not spent because of another program, that is, the use of UI funds for developmental training made the expenditure unnecessary. Surely it was financially prudent to allocate those funds to the refugee program.
As far as staff cuts are concerned, Mr. Chairman, I do not like them if they cause problems. Nevertheless, I reiterate my support for an excellent staff in the Department of Employment and Immigration. Surely, if the job is being done by existing staff, which is efficient, skilled, and has expertise, then one does not blindly charge on and suggest staff increases? That is not the financially prudent thing to do either.
If we can maintain our present level of service which, I suggest, is one of the highest in the world, then the present staff levels may well be adequate.
