Mr. Chairman, I would ask the minister a question regarding the Unemployment Insurance Commission. A problem has been brought to my attention which concerns a Mrs. Linda Huard, social insurance number 465 320 950. This lady was called for jury duty. She was on unemployment insurance and was reporting to the unemployment insurance office. She told the officials that she had been called for jury duty and had been selected. They told her to go ahead, but said that if it was for more than a day they would have to see what kind of ruling they could make. It so happened that the jury was empanelled for approximately five days. When she got home, she found a disentitlement notice saying that since she had been unavailable for work she was disentitled to benefits.
Would the minister clarify what seems to be a very foggy area with respect to individuals who set out, but do not know how long they will be empanelled on a particular case?

Mr. Chairman, that raises a very interesting point. I would be glad to receive details of that particular case. I am not sure in the interests of that individual whether it is in her or in the member's interest to discuss it on the floor of the House of Commons except by way of general concept in principle. I may say that I am one, above all, who would support the jury system and the onus that puts on a citizen as a condition of citizenship. If in fact there is a conflict between the obligation to serve as a juror, which is a very high obligation, in my opinion, and the rules of the Unemployment Insurance Commission, obviously I will be concerned. I will want to reconcile that in the interests of that person being allowed to do their duty as a citizen. I will undertake in that spirit to investigate that case to see if in fact there is a difficulty. I would suggest that that may well be a case for an appeal to the board of referees in the jurisdiction concerned.

With all due respect, I do not come here and name people's names unless I have their permission to do so in public. Let us get that on the record.
It is not good enough to tell Mrs. Huard or any other person in a like situation to go through the appeal process. That is not fair, Mr. Chairman. It is not fair at all. If the minister believes so much in the jury system and the responsibility of citizens to serve, then it is in his responsibility to send out a memo clarifying the whole area of those claimants on jury duty. That is your responsibility, Mr. Minister. Do not turn it around and tell citizens that they must go to the jungle of appeal processes. That is my first point.

November 16, 1979
Supply
I want a commitment from the minister that he will send a memo to his offices clarifying the whole question of jury duty and how it relates to those people who are receiving unemployment insurance.
Mr. Chairman, we do not need to waste a lot of time on this very important principle. It is one that I am very concerned about.
Send the memo.

And I would be pleased to discuss it with the hon. member. I do want to tell the hon. member that before 1 send memos I usually try to ascertain facts, and I will ascertain the facts and act accordingly.

Mr. Chairman, 1 want to get on to another question. 1 started this with the minister when we were in committee. It concerns overpayments. All we saw were headlines when the Auditor General came out with his report that $290 million was paid in overpayments. Immediately that banner headline in the newspapers was published, every citizen said that people on unemployment insurance were obviously ripping off the system.
As a matter of fact the Auditor General pointed out that $108 million of that overpayment was caused because employers incorrectly filled out the separation certificates. In such cases where this has created an overpayment, can the minister tell us this afternoon whether he intends to take any action with respect to getting those employers to pay the overpayment rather than going after the unemployed people to make restitution for something which was not their fault?

Mr. Chairman, as the hon. member well knows, those overpayments, which are very serious indeed and cause me concern both on account of the activities of employees and employers, are projections. It is not a very pretty picture, but I do want to tell him that the named individuals, that is, those who received the overpayments, are those in whom there may have been complicity, that is to say with employers who erroneously filled out forms. Those numbers are projections. We do not have the names in many cases of employers who actually filled out the forms wrongly that led to the overpayment.
If we have a situation of overpayment and we have identified the individual or we have identified the employer who may have deliberately filled out the form wrongly and we can spot it, then obviously the investigative personnel of the commission will take steps to recover the payment. That is a logical proposition and I accept that.
I do not want to mislead the hon. member or mislead the general public that we have thousands of names of employers who have wrongly filled out forms and we are going to go after them for the overpayments, because that is not a possibility. Rather, we have a system of establishing a new record of employment which is more detailed. This will take a great deal more time. We are going to insist that the employers fill out that form accurately. We believe that with that new form, with

proper promotion, and with the assistance of private sector groups-and I may say that I have had good co-operation from organizations such as the chamber of commerce and the Canadian Manufacturers' Association-we hope to reduce those instances of overpayment that are attributable to employer error. I think that is a legitimate goal, and I thank the hon. member again for drawing it to my attention.

Mr. Chairman, common to the minister on this topic, before I move on, is that it seems his department in past audits certainly had no difficulty in unearthing names of those individuals who have been overpaid. I would trust that the minister would be as assiduous in unearthing the names of those employers who the Auditor General, in his survey, says there is a potential for $108 million of overpayment due to their incorrectly filling out the separation certificates.
The other question I want to raise is one that touches on Canada Works. I represent a riding in northern Ontario. The minister well knows, as the former lawyer for Inco, the unemployment situation in the Sudbury basin. He knows well the yo-yo economy in which we exist in the Nickel Belt as in so many other parts of northern Ontario. He knows well that we do not have a proliferation of employers who could take advantage of the Local Employment Assistance Program. LEAP would work well if you had lots of employers in an area. But when you do not have lots of employers in an area which cannot take advantage of the local assistance program, what does this minister do? No sooner is he in office, his seat is not even warm, but holus-bolus he just wipes out northern Ontario from any Canada Works money, which is direct funding from the federal government into the municipalities.
I wrote to the minister. After waiting about three weeks and after much cajoling I finally got an answer, which was nothing but a lot of fluff. In effect he said to me that he has now set a surplus rate of 9 per cent, and we are below the surplus rate. The fact is that even his own office of unemployment for extended benefits uses 9.5 per cent. Today, as I stand in this House, that is the regional rate of unemployment in the Sudbury basin. But the minister does not go by the regional rate of unemployment. He goes by some concocted figure where all sorts of things were used to get it. Nine per cent became the cut-off point. This meant that all of northern Ontario has been eliminated from Canada Works.
We on this side of the House have never seen Canada Works as a solution to the unemployment problem in this country. Canada Works is not the solution, but it did provide jobs. Last year it provided several hundred jobs. In the absence of those jobs, these people will either be on unemployment insurance or welfare. The minister said he consulted with all sorts of people. It is no good to consult if you have blinkers on and your attitude is, "Don't confuse me with the facts or the realities of the situation."
I have here a letter dated November 6 from the Northern District Welfare Administration Boards which reads as follows:
November 16, 1979

Dear Mr. Rodriguez:
Please find attached a resolution unanimously passed by the six District Welfare Boards of Northern Ontario. The resolution is self-explanatory, but I would like to emphasize the extreme importance we attach to this resolution. All the northern boards are very concerned that this program's termination will have drastic effect on welfare costs. More importantly, we are concerned that the individuals who used this program to find dignity and independence will once again be forced to rely on public assistance.
We urge you to use whatever influence you may have to push for the replacement or reinstatement of the Canada Works program in our area.
I wish to read the resolution as well. I quote:
Resolution re: Federal government termination of Canada Works program in Ontario.
Whereas the Canada Works program provided needed employment to persons in rural and northern areas,
Whereas there is often no alternative employment in many northern and rural areas to this program,
Whereas the jobs provided under this program assisted many persons on general welfare in returning to work.
Whereas the termination of this program will mean increased costs in welfare expenditures.
Therefore be it resolved that the federal government be asked to reconsider the termination of this program or to replace this program with some other federal programs to provide employment in the northern and rural areas of Ontario.
It is obvious the minister did not involve himself in that kind of consultation. He did not consult the members of Parliament who represent those areas. He did not consult with me. 1 would have been very willing to give him the benefit of my experience in Nickel Belt. The minister knows Nickel Belt because he has been the lawyer for Inco.
Oh, oh!

The minister has been there many times to monitor hearings resulting from lay-offs in the nickel industry. He knows well the situation that exists in the Nickel Belt area of the Sudbury basin. However, what did he do? He eliminated the Canada Works program. He says we have LEAP, without examining the realities of putting LEAP in places where there is no proliferation of local employment opportunities.
He should look before he leaps.

That is what he should do. We know he speaks before he thinks. We have had experience with that. What the minister is doing in this situation is extremely serious, creating real hardship for many unable to get jobs through this program which, in the past, has been a good program.
The minister may be interested in knowing that the money for these programs often found its way into reforesting the area that his friends at Inco destroyed. Why would he bite the hand that fed him? That is beyond me. One would think he would not turn on his friends, but that is what he has done.
I want the minister to stand up now and say that he will reinstate the program in northern Ontario and in rural communities which do not have the opportunity to take advantage of the Local Employment Assistance Program. It is important
Supply
for the minister to come clean to the committee and tell us that.

Mr. Chairman, I am curious as to why the hon. member would downgrade a program like LEAP. If he were up to date on what is going on in his area, he would realize it will have considerable significance in northern Ontario. I wish to put on record some interesting statistics. Last year there was an allocation of $5.1 million for LEAP. Under this government there will be an allocation in Ontario, and 1 suggest most of it is going to northern Ontario, in the order of $10.2 million. The hon. member asks where the projects are in northern Ontario. I can tell him they are there. There are 21 projects approved and 56 projects planned.
I have had a number of meetings with people in the province of Ontario, in particular the minister, Mr. Bernier, who is very excited about LEAP as a vehicle to create long-term, not short-term jobs for the people of northern Ontario. Certainly there are problems getting three-year projects off the shelf, particularly when one is dealing with native communities. 1 appreciate that concern.
As a result of some initial start-up problems, we revised the regulation to create a transitional phase to permit those who had been operating within the Canada Works framework to develop their three-year projects, but to do that within a one-year period initially. That is in order not to preclude moneys that would be available for employment this winter.
I suggest the hon. member go back to the drawing board. He has been around here longer than I have. I had to go out and earn an honest living.
Order!
Oh, oh!

He stayed here and got somewhat out of touch as to what was going on in his community. In fact his community, like many others across the country, found that Canada Works was less than successful. As I indicated, it was expensive and it created short-term jobs. It would start up, it would end, and there would be nothing left. It is our objective to get people into the work force on a permanent basis.
I urge the hon. member to spend more time in Sudbury and Nickel Belt and talk to the people working with the LEAP program. He might find he likes it. That really is the answer to the problems of northern Ontario. I am delighted to say that as a result of consultations I have had, officials in the government of Ontario agree with me.

Mr. Chairman, I am glad the minister spent the last four or five years making an honest living. I noticed when he was answering me he had his hands in his pockets. He is the first lawyer 1 have ever seen with his hands in his own pockets.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Chairman, 1 think what is important at the outset is to indicate how the unemployment rate is determined for purposes of qualifying for Canada Works moneys. I think this is important not only for the hon. member but also for the previous speaker from the New Democratic Party. The criterion used is the same as that used by the previous government. It is called the labour surplus rate. It is not the unemployment insurance figure which is used in the monthly Statistics Canada bulletin.
What is done, because it is necessary to break it out by constituency-because that was the wish of hon. members and certainly the position of the previous government-is to determine the number of people on unemployment insurance by constituency. That can be determined simply through a determination of the postal code of the recipient of unemployment insurance. That number is taken as a percentage of the total labour force in a constituency as estimated by the Canada employment centres in the region. That gives us the labour surplus rate. If the figure is below 9 per cent, which this year is the trigger rate, then a constituency does not qualify. If it is above 9 per cent, then the amount of the allocation is proportionately increased depending on how high above 9 per cent the case may be.
In this case we have a situation where perhaps the labour surplus rate when determined was before a particular event took place, that is, the unfortunate lay-off of workers at IT and T Rayonier. That is the situation which, nevertheless, will have to be taken into account.

My second question relates to the problem of the Canada Works. What I would like to tell you, Mr. Minister, about that program, puts into question the integrity of the program and, unfortunately, it could put into question the reputation of the minister. The way that procedure has worked since its inception-and I think all members of the House could confirm it, on whatever side they may be-is that the civil servants in your department look into those projects, consult many people in the riding, get in touch with the member of Parliament and, if

Mr. Chairman, that is a very serious allegation indeed. Mr. Chairman, we have heard an interesting exchange which took up a lot of time. I do not think it proved anything, although I must admit that in my own constituency there was not a constituency advisory council in 1973. They were not introduced until 1974, although LIP and OFY had been in effect for two years or three years prior to that. They came into effect in 1974, and 1 set one up in my constituency. In fact, we were given the right to vote on that for the first two years. Then it was declared that the member was not entitled to sit or vote on constituency associations, and for the last three years we have not had a vote. Since I had gone to the trouble of setting up such an association I never presumed that I, over the ten or 13 people who were on this advisory group, should overrule their collective wisdom, and I never did overrule their collective wisdom.
I can remember on one occasion when I did write to the minister saying I certainly did not think that a certain program should go ahead. I was overruled by the minister, and it

went ahead regardless. That was only on one occasion, so I do know of an occasion at least in my own situation where a minister disagreed with what my advice and thoughts were, but by and large the constituency advisory group has been quite useful.
I know also, of course, that each year we talked about politicizing Canada Works, LIP and OFY, because it turned out often enough that Liberal cabinet ministers ended up getting larger shares than anybody else, and Liberal members, if you broke it out, always got more than Conservative members. It was just like decentralization. There was decentralization into 16 constituencies, 14 of which were represented by Liberals, and 11 of them by cabinet ministers. These things sometimes happen. It must be a freak of nature that they always happen that way.

Thank you for your assistance. I too, Mr. Chairman, would like through you to inform the minister that I would like to have the results of the regional economist for my constituency because we have got those results through one method or another before. We have also got results from each of the manpower offices, and 1 can tell you that in my constituency the results of the manpower offices and the results of the regional economist varied greatly, very, very greatly from what they call the labour surplus rate.
This labour surplus rate formula which was introduced by the previous administration under the directorship of Bud Cullen I have disagreed with entirely from the beginning. I shall explain why. If you are in a place of high unemployment-and you only have to go 50 miles up the Ottawa River on the Ontario side and you will find 15 per cent or 17 per cent unemployment-you do not have to go all the way to Matane, Labrador or Newfoundland, because there are pockets of high unemployment in Ontario and on the Quebec side of the Ottawa River. I want to tell the minister, and I hope he will pay attention, if you go by just the postal codes of those people who are getting cheques from unemployment insurance and you have a high rate of unemployment, there will be those who have gone through the entire period getting their cheques and using up all their weeks and have fallen off at the end who are not going to be counted any more because they are not getting cheques.
On the other hand, Mr. Chairman, if you have an area of high unemployment, the young people coming out of school cannot get jobs and they cannot put in enough weeks' work to ever get unemployment insurance, so they are not counted.
When you have those areas of higher unemployment, the ones who have used up their benefits and have fallen off at the

end, and their postal codes are not being churned out of the machine to give you the labour surplus rate, and those who have come out of school are young and have not been able to put in enough weeks to get laid off and receive cheques, will not be counted. That is why I have always disagreed with this program.
1 fought the former minister for three years on it. Eventually, after three years, he wrote me a letter and he partly agreed. He did not wholeheartedly agree but he partly agreed. I have always found their figures to be much higher than the labour surplus rate.

Mr. Chairman, those are concerns that I have shared with the hon. member previously. I can tell him that I am not happy with the labour surplus rate as the determinant of unemployment in a region. I think it is one of those factors that has developed under the previous government because of the insistence of the previous government that Canada Works moneys and Young Canada Works moneys and, before that, LIP moneys, be allocated by constituency, that is, the political boundaries. Apparently there was no other means devised of determining the unemployment within a constituency other than by the postal code and the labour surplus rate, with all of the imperfections the hon. member has so articulately put before the committee.
Were 1 proceeding on any new employment or job creation programs that were to be determined on a constituency by constituency basis I would be earnestly searching for an alternative that was an improvement. However, I can assure the hon. member that Canada Works is in its final phase. The new employment strategy of the government, to be announced on budget night, December 11, will indicate that we will put the money into those regions, not those constituencies but those regions that need it the most, on a more fair and more equitable basis, so the people who are truly unemployed can have the easiest and most convenient access to the money.

He was told by someone from the office of the Minister of Supply and Services that this dear minister who is looking after the interests of Quebeckers had obtained a postponement from his colleague, the Minister of Employment and Immigration, and

that his staff would have to work through the weekend to make a selection of the projects recommended by defeated Progressive Conservative candidates in Quebec, and moreover, that some projects already recommended by the department and for which the Liberal member of Parliament had given his approval would necessarily be rejected to provide the funds required for the projects submitted by Progressive Conservative friends.
This is the information that the secretary of a municipality was given by the secretary in the office of the Minister of Supply and Services. Mr. Chairman, 1 have no objection to seeing the Minister of Supply and Services play a special role in allocating funds set aside for the province of Quebec. He was elected, he is a minister of the Crown, he has special responsibilities, and I have no objection to his giving advice to his colleague. 1 think this is quite acceptable. He, the Minister of Supply and Services, so very candidly stated for all to hear after the last election that they intended to resort to patronage, that they had been in opposition long enough, that finally he would have an opportunity to do so and that he would hurry to do it.
What I do not accept from the Minister of Employment and Immigration is his current procrastination. He does not even have his colleague's candour and frankness to state squarely that, yes, patronage is rampant in his office, thanks to the complicity of officials from employment and immigration and from the office of the Minister for Supply and Services, that together they delayed for weeks projects that should have been approved for the province of Quebec, because they have not finished consulting with all the defeated Progressive Conservative candidates, and that very soon these funds will be approved and spent in Quebec. I wish he were frank and honest enough to state squarely that they are resorting to patronage. This afternoon, the minister in his protracted answers eluded the actual questions put to him in turn by the hon. members for Bonaventure-Iles-de-la-Madeleine, Manicouagan and Matapedia-Matane.
Every time those members asked him questions, he did not have the courage to confess publicly what his colleague, the Minister of Supply and Services, does not mind saying openly. He may be right, but then he may be wrong in being that open. It is for him to decide and for the people to judge. But at least he is honest enough to tell us openly what he is doing. 1 do not understand why the Minister of Employment and Immigration should not be that open. I find this program is too important and has too much impact on thousands of Canadians to play with words like that and waste the time of members by dodging the questions that are put to him.
Earlier the minister glossed over the fact that apparently a Progressive Conservative candidate submitted a project for over $200,000. In answer to the hon. member for Matapedia-
November 16, 1979

Matane, he said that the fact that someone has been a Conservative candidate should not stop him from submitting a project. Nobody ever denied anyone, even a defeated Conservative candidate, the right to submit a project, but what the hon. member for Matapedia-Matane wanted to know from the minister, and the minister did not answer him, is whether it is true that that Conservative candidate submitted a project for over $200,000, that the project was cut by Department of Employment and Immigration officials to at most $100,000 and following pressures made by that Conservative candidate, was going to be given the full amount in spite of and against the advice of his departmental officials. That is a very specific question, and yet the minister would not answer.
Once again, I put this on the same list of overwhelming facts that allow us to question the good faith, the good administration of that program. I add that to the unexplained abolition of advisory committees; I add that to the non-denial of lists of projects in every riding being sent to defeated Conservative candidates; and I add that to the desire of the minister to sweep that under the carpet today, and to try not to give straight answers to the legitimate questions put to him. I believe this program has been too important in the past for it to be so seriously compromised by a new administration.
Mr. Chairman, you will remember that when the Conservatives were in the opposition, they blamed the government for not solving the problem of unemployment in this country. They said at that time they were prepared to take over, they had all sorts of projects in mind to fight unemployment efficiently. Well, they are now in power. They have formed this government for over six months, and curiously, those people when they were sitting over here on the left of the Speaker, were full of ideas and projects. Since they have formed the government and sat to the right of the Speaker, they no longer seem to have any ideas, any projects, any bright ideas about solving the problems of unemployment in this country. The facts are there, Mr. Speaker. Since that party formed the government, no new job-creation program has been launched in this country. Some programs in effect under the previous Liberal government have been cut. A program which I find as important as the on the job training program has been cut by the Conservative government. Other important programs have experienced substantial budgetary cuts, such as the Canada Works program.
I think, Mr. Chairman, that this arbitrary decision of the Progressive Conservative government to cut off the minimum funds made available to every constituency in Canada is unfair to some Canadians living in constituencies that have not as much unemployment as in others, but where there is surely some hardship and problems and where a program such as the Canada Works program could be quite effective.
All allowances have been cut in my constituency of Papi-neau. For a few years we had been receiving an average of $400,000 to $450,000 a year enabling hundreds of individuals
Supply
to work, and especially several hundreds of others to receive some care or services which would not have otherwise been provided.
The minister tells us that the Canada Works program does not meet his criteria as a permanent job-creation program. He tells us we have to trust the private sector which should replace the state as a provider of stable employment in our market economy. I say to the minister that he erred when he cut, as he did, the Canada Works program in 33 Quebec ridings, and in particular, in the riding of Papineau, because all sorts of people were benefiting from its advantages, people who now live under the threat of no longer receiving those advantages, and who cannot bank on private enterprise for the same services.
1 am thinking in particular of a project which, last year, got some $30,000 for a social, cultural and family centre designed to enable people to take warm meals to the aged in their homes, to help them with their housecleaning, and give them a bit more comfort and assistance than they normally get. Private enterprise will never offer that type of service. Private enterprise will never replace the Canada Works program to dispense that kind of help.
Yet the Canada Works program assistance was drastically reduced in the riding of Papineau, depriving hundreds of senior citizens of that very interesting and important service, which not only helped them but also gave employment to a score or more persons in my riding.
There is another project, and I shall close on that note, Mr. Chairman, which deals with the re-integration of the alcoholic in his work environment, this one outside my riding. The Montreal AAA received, thanks to the Canada Works program, a substantial amount to perform essential work in that field; it may no longer receive any grants since the program was cut in my riding; not one single penny has been spent in Papineau because of the inhuman, irresponsible and unacceptable attitude of the Minister of Employment and Immigration.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The time of the hon. member has expired. The hon. member for Kamloops-Shuswap.

Mr. Chairman, I was beginning to think I was going to get blown right by five o'clock. However, I do want to ask a couple of questions of the minister. First, I will describe my riding a little bit because I know the minister has not seen it. It is a riding consisting of about 200 miles north and south, and about 175 miles east and west. T'he main centre is Kamloops. While the citizens of Kamloops can stand on their feet at all times and expect no help, I do have in my outlying ridings many small communities. People living in these communities work for the main in the logging industry, sometimes they do a little prospecting in the summer, and

November 16, 1979
Supply
there are a few trappers. I wonder could these people qualify for LEAP money?
In my area we also have a lot of Indian reserves. The people in the Indian reserves are generally the first ones out of work. Could the minister take a close look to see if he could help them in any way?

Mr. Chairman, I can reply to the hon. member for Kamloops-Shuswap by saying that yes, both trappers and natives, Indians and Metis, can qualify for the LEAP program.
Indeed, I think in his part of the country, the interior of British Columbia, the LEAP program is ideally suited to serving the needs of those communities, for two reasons. First, it is related to employment that is meaningful. In a sense it is related to economic assistance in projects that produce real goods and services and make a contribution to the economy and are not simply make-work projects.
Second, and perhaps equally important, it provides a vehicle for long-term employment, up to three years. It is not the "start-stop" type of operation which has plagued government job creation at the federal level in that part of the world for so long. I would encourage the hon. member through his local office at the Canada Employment Centre to make contact on behalf of his constituents to provide whatever assistance he may seek.
I may take this opportunity to answer some of the concerns that the lengthy speech of my friend opposite prevented me from doing. I may say that I find it surprising that the hon. member for Papineau seems to take objection to the notion that lists of projects that are valid and legitimate projects forthcoming from a region, some with the concurrence of MPs and some without their concurrence, having been assessed by project officers of mine, should somehow be kept in secret.
1 want to make the hon. member an offer to indicate the openness of approach, and consistent with the position I indicated to him, that I take all the information I can get. 1 seek all the advice I can get. If the defeated candidates in the riding of Joliette or in the riding of Brome-Missisquoi or in the riding of Lotbiniere wish to come to my office or to go through the hon. member for Joliette-
Oh, oh!

-to obtain the information, I would be delighted to make the projects from that particular constituency available for their information and to invite their recommendations. I say this in all seriousness, Mr. Chairman. I think that a person who has run for office in a constituency, whether he be Conservative, Liberal, Creditiste, or NDP, knows a little bit about the constituency from which an application may come. As long as we have a Canada Works program-and this is the last phase-that is based on constituency allocation and is designed for projects that will be useful to the community to provide employment in the community, I am going to seek advice from every single source which cares to give me advice. I think that is consistent with the philosophy of the program

and I make no apology for having sought advice from a great many sources.
It is interesting that the hon. member for Papineau should seek to give me a lecture on the art of patronage.
Oh, oh!
Why not? He knows a lot about it.

I am tempted to say that he should be a good teacher in his own right. I only have to make reference to the very successful career of one of his own friends and assistants who, with the assistance of the hon. member when he was a minister, had a rather meteoric ride in the public service of Canada in a way in which I would never suggest was patronage, but nevertheless reflected the very close interest and assistance of the hon. member when he was a minister. The gentleman to whom I made reference was a former member of this House in the period 1968 to 1972. On his defeat in 1972 he became an executive assistant to the minister where he trained for the next election, which he fought and lost in a Toronto constituency in 1974. I am sure there was no element of patronage in this. For his efforts he was given the position of vice-chairman of the Farm Credit Corporation. He served in that position for a period of three years. Not to be outdone by that particular effort, the same individual was promoted in 1978 to chairman of the Egg Marketing Board.
The farmer's friend.

The same individual carried through with the assistance of the minister right up until one month ago when, for some strange reason, through some happy consequence of events, the true mettle of that gentleman-the friend of the former minister-was found out. Not only could he not get along with the board of directors of the Egg Marketing Board, but he could not get along with the government, for reasons which are still strange to me. I suspect it may have had something to do with his salary, but I do say it is exceedingly strange that the hon. member opposite should lecture me, a newcomer to this House, on the subtle art of patronage.
Oh, oh!

Let me get back to unemployment and assisting the unemployed people of this country.
It is funny that the hon. member makes the same mistake as did one of his predecessors, the hon. member for Blainville-Deux-Montagnes who indicated that this government had put forward no programs to assist the unemployed. I ask him the same question I asked the hon. member for Nickel Belt: have you ever heard of a LEAP program? This is the Local Employment Assistance Program. It is just a small amount of money, $18 million this year, $12 million next year, which is there to assist the people who need it. I do not know whether any of that LEAP money is going into the Papineau riding. I suggest a great proportion is going into the province of Quebec. Quite apart from that, I wonder if the hon. member could tell me in last year's Canada Works allocation what
November 16, 1979

portion of the national allocation to Canada Works went into the province of Quebec? I would suggest that if he checks the figures he would find it is about one-third. About one-third of the money under the previous government went to the province of Quebec. That is fair. I will give the hon. member that. It is fair because Quebec has a population of about one-third of the total population of Canada. It is reasonable that Quebec will get one third of the total dollars.
What does the new government do, having an opportunity to assess Canada Works in a time of restraint, to maintain a program to provide jobs for the unemployed this winter? The new government is providing 48.7 per cent of a total allocation of Canada Words for the province of Quebec. That is a significant improvement in a proportional sense. I would suggest that it is an indication of our commitment to fight unemployment in that province.
I would suggest, notwithstanding that the hon. member feels deprived in Papineau, that the increased allocation in proportionate terms together with the broader advice that this government is seeking and receiving as to good projects throughout the constituencies that need them, that the successs of the program this year will exceed anything ever achieved by the previous government.
In conclusion, I think the remarks of the hon. member for Papineau about the private sector's involvement in job creation really do indicate, for all concerned to see, the difference in philosophy between this government and the previous one. I am not sure I fully understand the gist of the hon. member's remarks. I heard him say something to the effect that the private sector really cannot create the jobs that are necessary. He said something to the effect that the private sector cannot provide meaningful jobs. Let me tell him that is a difference. 1 am glad he said that.
I want to assure him that job-creation projects, employment strategies from the government, at present will rely on the private sector. We will do that for a variety of reasons. First, the jobs created under this government in the private sector will be permanent jobs, not start-stop, make-work jobs that disappear like a bit of air in the night. They will be lasting jobs that are meaningful for people.
Second, let me tell the hon. member something about the cost of job creation. If he examined the records, and I would be pleased to provide the information, he would see that Canada Works for job creation is one of the most expensive programs that any federal government has ever put forward.
If we are really concerned about cost effectiveness, which this government is, we will try to get the greatest value for the dollar being spent to try to help as many people as possible. I suggest to the hon. member in those phases of Canada Works that attempted to provide minimum constituency levels, while it may have made his job easier because he had $150,000 to hand out in Papineau or wherever, it did not help the unemployed in the areas where they needed it the most.
Supply
In this case we have applied the available resources to those constituencies with the highest unemployment rate. That is the position that has been recognized throughout the country as the final one.
I should mention that there is one group in this whole process who have yet to be mentioned. What about the provincial governments? Where do they stand in all this? They, of course, have responsibilities in the field of job creation and an obligation to sustain welfare costs. Like all levels of government, they would prefer to have people work rather than be on welfare. We share that goal.
I have engaged in two extensive, comprehensive federal-provincial consultations with my ten provincial counterparts in the labour manpower field. They are unanimous in telling me that Canada Works is a program which should be terminated. It is a program that is political in nature, expensive, distorts provincial spending priorities, creates expectations that can never be met, is inefficient and should be ended.
We have had unanimous support from across the country for that position. Nevertheless, in the face of very high unemployment in regions of Canada like Quebec, the four Atlantic provinces, and to a certain extent British Columbia, we have maintained that program one more time for the purpose of this winter, for which we make no apology.
There will be an opportunity on December 11 because the full details of the new government's approach to employment strategy will be fully revealed and discussed before the Canadian people. 1 want to emphasize three points that will be the underlying philosophy of that program which will be available this winter as a new program to help the unemployed of Canada.
First, our emphasis will be on the creation of long-term jobs. We are not interested in short-term job creation which is expensive and does not really help anyone. Second, there must be a concerted effort to help the youth of Canada, those 24 and under who find themselves without jobs, who in fact cannot get that first job and are fast in danger of becoming another generation of unemployed drawing unemployment insurance.
The final point, and I again emphasize this, is that this government will rely on the private sector to create the real jobs in this society. We believe that through the employment tax credit system announced in the throne speech we will be able to create more permanent jobs, jobs that will last a longer period of time. That is the way to go, and that is the way this government will be going.

speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, followed by Bill C-20. I do not see the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie) in the chamber. Because he had some problems with respect to meetings this afternoon, the minister came in to inform the House as soon as he could of the date of the budget. There was some question about whether that would be appropriate during the course of committee proceedings. The Minister of Finance felt he should do it as quickly as he could. I wish to confirm now that the Mace is on the Table the advice given to the committee this afternoon, that a budget will brought down on December 11, 1979.
[ Translation\

Mr. Speaker, I thank the President of the Privy Council and Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Baker) for informing the House that the government has decided to bring down its budget on December 11. I rose on a point of order earlier this afternoon because 1 would have appreciated if the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie) had had the courtesy to inform members representing the opposition parties of his intention of announcing in the House the date of the budget. I think that he has somewhat abused parliamentary procedures by defiantly interrupting the debates of the Committee of the Whole, without even waiting for the Chairman to recognize
him, rising decisively to advise us that the budget will be brought down December 11 and leaving forthwith.
All I can say is that Liberals are very happy to see that the government will at last be introducing its budget. We have been expecting it for a long time, and we dare hope it will not be a Santa Claus with an empty bag who will be here just before Christmas, but that this budget will satisfy the needs of working poor, senior citizens and all those who are affected by the undue rise in interest rates and the thoughtless increases in the price of oil in Canada.

As Acting Minister of Finance, I would like to assure the hon. member that we will make the best of the situation the former government left us with. The budget will certainly be a great improvement over the November 16 budget.
No more excuses. Take your own responsibility.

Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to ask the government House leader a question. With the budget coming down on December 11, can he assure this House that the budget debate, which I believe takes six days, will be six consecutive days, or can he tell us now what the order of that debate will be?
